M O R E   M A I L ! !


    March, 1992      Page Reply

 How to write to us...02     -
 Susan Harvey.........03    09
 C. Grant Dixon.......15    17
 Simon Strange........19    21
 Malcolm Goodman......23    28
 Malcolm Wright.......29    38
 Miles Kinloch........39    47
 Dave Smith...........50    52
 J. Cary..............53    54

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: Susan Harvey, ESSEX

Dear Ron and Brian,

Thank you very much for the +D
and disc drive which arrived
last month.

When I ordered the +D I was not
sure how well it would work with
my Spectrum +2A as I heard
rumours that it only worked in
48K mode. However, Datel
provided an adaptor that goes
between the +D and the computer,
and also a POKE @ to enable the
+D to be used in +3 BASIC mode.

It works fine, and my sons were
soon using the snapshot button
to transfer games from tape to
disc.

This is a big advantage when
128K games can take up to 10
minutes to load from tape. Using
OUTLET with the disc drive is a
real pleasure; it all loads so
quickly and reliably.

To use the +D with +3 BASIC, I
first load the system file and
then type:
  POKE @4426,16 : POKE @4427,92

 ...and reset the computer to +3
BASIC. I can now use the +3
editor (which I find much easier
than 48K) and also the RAM disc
and parallel printer port. Both
the disc operating system and
the POKE @ remain in the memory
after pressing the reset button,
which makes it all very easy to
use.

The handbook was very helpful in
getting started and all was
going well until I tried to type
in:
    SAVE d1 q$
and the computer refused to
accept it. This seemed odd as -
SAVE d1 "program" - worked fine.
A quick look through my OUTLET
disc showed the solution to be:

    SAVE d1;q$.

I then realised that to get the
most from the +D disc system, I
need more information. The hand-
book is very good as far as it
goes but is really only an
introduction. It mentions both
FORMAT and INDUG but gives no
addresses for them.

Can you recommend any particular
back issues of OUTLET to help in
using and programming the +D or
any other useful sources of
information?

Any information on disc drives
in general would also be helpful
- for example:- the +D manual
mentions cleaning the heads on
the drive, but as the drive
itself has no manual, I have no
idea how to do this.

The only real problem, I have
found so far is that while the
system will recognise both the
RAM disc and the parallel
printer port, it will not do so
immediately after using the disc
drive.

For example...

10 LOAD d1"textfile" CODE x,y
20 FORMAT LPRINT "U"

      ...loads the file and then
produces the response: "NONSENSE
IN G+ DOS". The only way I have
found to get round this is to
insert -line 15 STOP. Then, when
the STOP report occurs, type
GOTO 20 or CONTINUE.

Having a disc drive makes using
the computer a lot easier and
much more fun. I recommend any-
one with a SPECTRUM+2A to stop
waiting for Amstrad to produce
the mythical SI-1 disc interface
and obtain a +D and disc drive
as soon as possible (Make sure
it is the +2A version).

Very many thanks Ron & Brian for
recommending and providing my
great disc drive. Keep up the
marvellous work with OUTLET.

        Yours sincerely,

          Mrs S.Harvey

P.S. Did you know your yellow
wallets are just too narrow to
accept computer paper?

Brian Cavers to Susan Harvey

INDUG is INDEPENDANT DISCIPLE/+D
USER GROUP and FORMAT is its
monthly magazine. However they
now cover the Spectrum and SAM
generally and are not restricted
to just the Disciple or +D. I am
not sure if the title INDUG has
thus been dropped and FORMAT
adopted. The address is 34
Bourton Road,Gloucester,GL4 0LE.

Regarding OUTLET back issues, I
guess much Disciple/+D info and
drive use generally is swapped
in these OUTLETTERS pages so it
is worth looking back through
the issues you have to re-read
them as you probably would not
have absorbed the info before.

I don't keep an index of subject
matter coming up in OUTLETTERS
other than a short list of items
of special interest. Other items
well worth looking at are:
"UNITRANS+" (OUTLET 20) for
transferring software from tape
to disc; DRIVECHAT in OUTLET 23
has an excellent article by
Grant Dixon on the way programs
are stored on Disciple/+D disc;
DISCVIEW (OUTLET 28), SEEKN'PEEK
(OUTLET 45) and DISCSEARCH
(OUTLET 51) all examine discs
while CATLOADER (OUTLET 44) is a
MUST for loading and selective
erasing, copying and renaming.

Meanwhile, please write if you
want clarification on a specific
area of using drives; I'll be
glad to try to help.

If anyone else is interested in
doing an article or articles on
using the Disciple/+d or using
drives in general then I'll be
happy to put them in DRIVECHAT.

Now,regarding cleaning the drive
heads, this is done by inserting
a special cleaning disc. I'm not
sure of a supplier (does anyone
else know?). However,this should
not apply to you for a long time
because you have new drives and
in any event, I have never used
one and do not intend to unless
I really think it necessary.

The yellow wallets are made from
standard A4-size card(to fit the
standard envelopes) but the edge
fixing reduces the internal size
(tuck A4 sheets under the flap).

The problem with using FORMAT
LPRINT "U" with a +D attached is
tricky! I don't think the POKE
23728 idea I suggested before is
of use. It may help to set BIT 2
of 23398 before using the FORMAT
LPRINT. How?...

I've written a short routine for
you which is in this issue as
"BITPOKER". If you load the
program, press E to extract the
routine then alter the line
number to 15(delete the old line
at 9999) and save it then merge
it into your program. Alter the
LET P=55555 to... LET P=23398.
Alter the bit to be set to bit 2
by changing LET B=7 to LET B=2
and the LET S$="1" sets the bit
so can be left unchanged.

It's just occured to me that the
line 1001 in our loader program
may (also?) solve the problem.It
is well worth trying. See my
reply to Bill Coats in the next
block of OUTLETTERS after this
for more details.

Let me know the results but if
it doesn't work then the only
thing I can think of is to get a
standard BBC printer cable and
use the +D printer port. You can
get such a cable for `7.99 + `1
postage from PBT ELECTRONICS LTD
Port Talbot Workshops, Unit 17,
Addison Road, Port Talbot SA12
6HZ (Tel: 0639 885008). Ask for
a "Parallel printer cable for a
+D" and, as ever, always tell
suppliers that you heard of them
in OUTLET!

If you do use the +D's own print
output then re-study your +D
manual on using a printer as you
may need to POKE @ to customise
it how you want it and then
resave the DOS.
                       - Brian

From: C.Grant Dixon, ROSS-ON-WYE

Dear Brian,

I wonder if you, or possibly an
OUTLET reader, can help me. I
purchased a legitimate copy of
'OMNICALC TWO' and I am having a
bit of trouble running it on my
system.

Although it supports larger
printers and the text is indeed
getting through to my printer
there is no auto-linefeed and it
is all printed on one line. I
DON'T want to alter dip switches
every time I use the program. I
have tried to break into the
BASIC with MERGE and STOP but
the program seems to be well
protected.

Also I want to save the screen.
I tried using the Disciple
screen snapshot command which is
supposed to return you back to
the program with the screen
intact. Unfortunately,it returns
you back after wiping the entire
memory so that you have lost all
the data, and the program.

I have succeeded once in snap-
shotting the screen but on other
occasions the disaster occurred.

It looks a good program if it
would work properly and I would
be grateful for any suggestions.
I am using a Spectrum + with
Disciple interface feeding 5.25"
and 3.5" disc drives DSDD and a
Panasonic KXP-1081 printer. Hope
you can help.       Yours, Grant

To Grant Dixon from Ron Cavers

As far as I know, there is no
way of adding commands to the
controlling basic in Omnicalc -
even if you break into the BASIC
(which I have done). However,
you can get round the problem by
adding your own "front-end"
BASIC - as follows:


 50 REM Insert your printer
    commands here

100 FOR F=USR "A" TO USR "A"+2:
    READ A: POKE F,A: NEXT F:
    RANDOMISE USR USR "A": LOAD
    D1"om2": DATA 207,49,201

200 SAVE D1"AUTOLOAD" LINE 1

Save this onto a blank disk and
then add your Omnicalc program -
alter line 100 above if you are
using om64000. (If I remember
correctly, om64000 creates a
program called "run" and this
could be loaded from line 100.

The remainder of line 100 is to
call the Spectrum ROM and get it
to set up the system variables
as for Interface 1. This is
sufficient to trick Omnicalc
into behaving as though the
microdrives are present and will
thus allow you to use your disk
drives. Hope this helps.   RON

From: Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS


Brian/Ron

This may be 'old hat' but since
I don't have any SAM-specific
copies of OUTLET I write anyway.

Being new to the SAM computer,
one of the first things I did
was get it working like a
Spectrum. Further examination of
the paging code made me aware
that it should be possible to
put a copy of the Spectrum ROM
at address 0 but with the
ability to poke, and alter, any
ROM addresses. I, therefore,
tried this out and found that
indeed it did work.

However, in the process I
discovered that data corruption
occured in the character set and
also in locations 0 to 4, and
this warranted investigation.

The offending bits of code
reside at locations 3372 and
13308/9.

The solution was quite simple.

Firstly, load a copy of the
Spectrum's ROM into the SAM at
65536.

Then 'POKE 68908,23', DPOKE
78844,19

Next enter the following code in
line 9999:-

POKE 50000,1250,35,237,65,1,252,
4,237,65,199: CALL 50000

In a few moments your SAM
becomes a Spectrum and you can
alter ROM addresses to your
heart's content.

One small restriction: don't try
putting anything into locations
19 to 23 inclusive as these will
be altered as the Spectrum runs.

Apart from this you can now POKE
to ROM addresses to see what
results.

NOW HERE'S A ROUTINE FOR THE
SPECTRUM WHICH MAY BE OF
INTEREST...

On the SAM there is a command
'INPUT #2;"name";a$', which
results in the prompt appearing
on the upper screen. Well, now
we can have something comparable
for the Spectrum. I've done it
all in BASIC so that more users
can see what's happening...

10 LET a=PEEK 23631+256*peek
23632.

20 POKE a+7,168: POKE a+8,16

30 INPUT#2;"name ";#0;a$: PRINT
a$

40 INPUT#2;"age ";#0;b$:PRINT b$

50 INPUT#2;"sex ";#0;c$:PRINT c$
and so on.

As you will see, if you run
this, the prompt will appear on
the upper screen. Your response
will be entered on the lower
screen and will then be printed
in the upper screen adjacent to
the prompt.

An excellent way of entering
multiple inputs.

You could try omitting the #0 in
these lines but the results get
very messy and need lots of ''''
to tidy it up. you also get lots
of cursors printed !!.

           Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

Thanks, Malcolm. I shall have to
experiment a bit with that input
routine.

As for Spectrum emulators on the
SAM, there are numerous ones (we
have had two in OUTLET) but it's
interesting to see it presented
in this way. What fascinated me
here is this corruption. The
reason why I think nobody(?) has
been aware of this is that it is
possible on the SAM to "WRITE
PROTECT" the RAM in the first
page so that even machine code
cannot write to it. This is done
by setting bit 7 of the low
memory page register (port 250).
                        - Brian

From: Malcolm Wright, CO. DURHAM

I used to have one of these
printers. It wasn't mine, just a
loan from a friend. What I used
to do was run it from my 48K
SPECCY using a KEMPSTON "E"
interface as this had the appro-
priate driver in ROM or rather
EPROM hence the name. I tried it
on the SAM and got various
strange results.

I now have an AMSTRAD DMP 2000,
and share an OLIVETTI DM124c
24-pin colour printer with my
brother.

You are correct in assuming that
CHR$ 0 is the escape code for
the GPA 100A.

It will work satisfactorily with
the SAM only if all driver soft-
ware is "custom" made. Spare
ribbons for this machine are
available cheaply from RIBBONS
DIRECT. I've lost their address
but a quick check in the trade
magzines will get you this. (See
my notes on re-inking later).

At one time SEIKOSHA made this
printer for TANDY under the
RADIO SHACK brand.An upgrade ROM
used to be available for the
printer to allow faster draft
speed and NLQ. These printers
were the mainstay of many an
office at one time but now, with
their odd standard parallel/
Centronics interface and non-NLQ
text they are a little anti-
quated.

Don't get me wrong - they are a
very good and robust printer if
you don't mind the limitations.

SEIKOSHA (SEIKO/EPSON) are a bit
"funny" to deal with when it
comes to after-sales service. If
you're not a BIG concern they
treat you with little respect.
So, if you have problems with
this or other SEIKOSHA printers,
don't say I didn't warn you.

On the subject of printers, any-
one who has problems with the
"muddy yellow" syndrome there is
a simple solution. Always remem-
ber the following golden rule:-

Dark TO light is never right,
Dark ON light is better.

I.e., print white, then yellow,
then cyan, then magenta and
lastly black. This way the
lighter inks don't pick up the
darker ones. It's easy when you
think about it.


I got the idea watching a four-
colour lithographic system in
use. It also applies to some
silk screen printing proccesses!


Now if only the chaps who write
printer drivers would learn this
rule I might not need to keep
buying expensive ribbons..

A little explaining of how my
BAR SCROLL [SAM OUTLET 52] works
would not go amiss here so....

M$ contains the message A$ is
the array which contains the
font LOGO$ contains my ZAEON
logo chr$ 13 (carriage return)
fast clear of text on bar chr$
129 bar wipe up/down chr$ 137
colour rotate chr$ 142 put my
logo in center of bar TASWORD
save its files as code so mem$
these out and remove all the
"padding" spaces and add a chr$
13 at the end of each line.

It's fairly simple to write a
routine to do this. You could
use other graphic chr$ to do
other fx if you like; I leave
that up to you.

Any reader can use the scroller
in his/her progs; just give me a
small mention.

The technique I used to wipe the
bar up and down in the LOGO DEMO
[OUTLET 50](yes,it DID only take
20 mins to write, I had some
routines in stock so to speak
from a simple SPECTRUM version)
was to OUT values from 0 to 191
into port 249.

A quick check in the SAM
TECHNICAL MANUAL will tell you
that this handles the line
position of a palette change in
palette 0. This makes a bouncing
horizon a breeze from BASIC just
try OUTing random values in this
can be hilarious.

Onto the subject of re-inking
(black!) ribbons. I have two
printers at my disposal normally
but one is out on loan. One is
an AMSTRRAD DMP2000 (same as the
3000 and 3160) and the other a
24 pin colour printer an
OLIVETTI DM124c.

I tend to re-ink my AMSTRAD
ribbons as these are the easiest
to get at. The mixture I have
found that works the best (some
dry up too quickly) is STEPHENS
endorsing or stamp pad ink,a
drop of washing-up liquid and a
drop or two of WD40 or TANDY's
RECISION OILER lubricant (this
is a TEFLON based liquid).
ALLWAYS SHAKE the mixture a
little before applying to the
ribbon.

In the case of my machine I
found that attaching a nozzle
from a used can of WD40 to the
ink bottle,which is plastic and
squeezy, I could apply the
mixture direct to the ribbon
without getting too messy.

Remember to put the printer into
self-test while doing this, and
let it run till the desired
quality of print is achieved
without getting the ribbon
totally drenched in ink.

The reason for the WD40 in the
mixture is purely to prevent the
ink clogging up the print head,
the washing-up liquid helps to
prevent the ink drying out too
quickly on the ribbon.

So far this has worked exceed-
ingly well. Other types of
ribbon may have to be done in a
different manner but if you use
the nozzle technique you don't
get yourself too dirty. I am not
sure if anyone makes yellow,
cyan or magenta stamp pad inks,
but if they do then I'll try
doing a colour ribbon next. I'll
let you know how I get on.

Thank you for producing the BEST
mag around for BOTH the SAM and
SPECTRUM.

         Malcolm Wright

Dear Brian,
I have a few programming hints
and tips which might interest
other readers, so thought I'd
write in to share them. To begin
with, I'd like to pass on two
very useful pieces of inform-
ation I received from a fellow
OUTLET reader,Karl-Heinz Meander
from Germany, who suggested I
could forward them to you.

The first of these consists of
two POKEs for 'Wordmaster' which
will delete all files at once,
saving having to do each one
individually:

POKE 65532,158: POKE 65533,96.

These can be included permanent-
ly as a final line in the 'Word-
master' BASIC for convenience.

Secondly, Karl-Heinz has
discovered two undocumented
system variables in RAM page 7
of the 128K Spectrum which hold
the colours used for the 128K
Editor and Opening Menu. These
can be altered from BASIC by a
routine such as he suggests:-

10 CLEAR 49151 (or less)
20 POKE 23388,23 (page in Ram 7)
30 POKE 60431,main menu
   attribute byte
40 POKE 60433,editor attribute
   byte
50 POKE 23388,16 (page in
   Ram 0)
60 CLEAR 65367 (or whatever...)

Alternatively, I thought it
might be an idea to set up these
variables from machine-code, as
this would get round the need to
CLEAR 49151 first - not always
convenient if included in a long
program.

I have, therefore, written a
short routine to demonstrate
this [in ADD-ENDERS]then instead
of having to work out the value
of the attribute byte yourself,
it is taken directly from ATTRP
(23693).

All you need do, then, is set up
the PAPER and INK commands as
normal, then GOSUB 9910 (the
line no. can be changed) which
will make the colours in the
128K Editor & Menu the same.

(Please note, however, that even
though this method makes it
unnecessary to alter RAMTOP, the
code in line 9910 still has to
be below 49152 when called, to
avoid paging itself out.)

Incidentally, the purpose of the
variables temp1 and temp2 is for
48K compatibility, so that these
locations will not be corrupted
if paging does not take place.

What I cannot be certain of is
whether these RAM 7 POKEs will
work on +2A/+3 Spectrums, since
Karl-Heinz, like myself, has the
older type of 128K machine.
(Perhaps you could let me know
if it works on your own +3? I'd
be interested to know.)

The other matter I wanted to
mention concerns a peculiar
hardware bug which affects
certain Amstrad-made Spectrums
(the grey +2s in particular)
with certain programs, since it
affected '$KIPPER' in the last
issue. I have added a bit on to
$KIPPER to overcome this problem
on such machines.[In ADD-ENDERS]

Some people with grey +2s may
have noticed that in 48 mode
certain keys sometimes fail to
respond as they should, namely
the right and up arrow keys,
caps shift/m, caps shift/n and
symbol shift/a. Certain
interfaces, particularly the
Kempston Mouse, exacerbate the
problem.

An intriguing fact, however, is
that the symptoms are worst when
the machine is first switched
on, and gradually diminish as it
warms up! I cannot shed much
light on the actual cause of
this, except to say that I once
read somewhere that it was due
to a bug in the ULA chip.

I discovered,through experiment,
that the 'I' register plays an
important role in these
phenomena (though why this
should be, I have no idea). When
'I' holds zero, the symptoms
disappear completely. If 'I'
holds 63, the arrow keys are not
affected (at least on my
machine), though the other keys
I mentioned are.

If 'I' holds other values, the
trouble is worst - hence the
problem with $KIPPER on these
machines (in 48 mode) - it uses
interrupts and inhibits proper
operation of these vital keys!
My solution was to 'patch' a
piece of code into the routine,
temporarily loading 'I' with
zero before calling the ROM key-
scan (RST 56),which has cured
the problem, at least for me.
I shall find $KIPPER very useful
as I frequently use the 48K
editor for embedded codes,
tokens etc. I don't know if
you've heard of these effects
before, but I know of other
programs where these problems
have arisen, and other people
who have experienced them -
notably with 'Wordmaster'.

(Incidentally, I wrote a 'patch'
for Wordmaster to deal with this
- if anyone wants it, please
write to me with SAE.) I suspect
many people probably (wrongly,
though understandably) assume
these things to be program bugs,
whereas in reality it's the
machine itself which is to
blame.

(I wonder, does this also affect
the +3 and +2A, or is it just
the grey +2 models?)

Anyway, hope you will find these
things useful, and keep up the
good work.

            Regards,

          Miles Kinloch

From Brian Gaff to Miles Kinloch

Thanks for the information about
page 7 system variables. These
ring a bell, as when I was
supplying software for Micronet,
I had a program sent to me
called Megayuck, which changed
the 128K colours to green on
magenta! Yuck indeed!

Yes they do work on the +2A and
+3 with one slight modification.
You need to wait for an
interrupt when doing it from
BASIC. This is easily done by
adding a PAUSE 1 in line 20.

The grey +2 keyboard quirks are
well known, as Amstrad refused
to admit to them, which annoyed
the Sinclair mags, as I recall.

I think the problem is one of
timings in the two-key rollover
routine. The Amstrad keyboards
seem to use electronics to give
pre-shifted keys, whereas the
old 128K had a multi-layer
membrane.

It's interesting about the mouse
interface though, as we have a
letter this month, describing
this effect, which I must admit,
I have not encountered.

The newer +3 and +2A machines
have a different keyboard fault.
In these machines, the two key
rollover routine seems to miss
the shift at times, so that the
pre-shifted keys can give their
unshifted values!

I spoke to Cliff Lawson of
Amstrad some time ago about all
these problems, and he suggested
that a fix had been developed,
but it involved actually re-
writing the keyboard scanning
ROM routines, and this screwed

As far as I know, there is no way of adding commands to the controlling basic in Omnicalc - even if you break into the BASIC (which I have done). However, you can get round the problem by adding your own "front-end" BASIC - as follows:

50 REM Insert your printer commands here

100 FOR F=USR "A" TO USR "A"+2: READ A: POKE F,A: NEXT F: RANDOMISE USR USR "A": LOAD D1"om2": DATA 207,49,201

200 SAVE D1"AUTOLOAD" LINE 1

Save this onto a blank disk and then add your Omnicalc program - alter line 100 above if you are using om64000. (If I remember correctly, om64000 creates a program called "run" and this could be loaded from line 100.

The remainder of line 100 is to call the Spectrum ROM and get it to set up the system variables as for Interface 1. This is sufficient to trick Omnicalc into behaving as though the microdrives are present and will thus allow you to use your disk drives. Hope this helps.   RON

Brian/Ron

This may be 'old hat' but since I don't have any SAM-specific copies of OUTLET I write anyway.

Being new to the SAM computer, one of the first things I did was get it working like a Spectrum. Further examination of the paging code made me aware that it should be possible to put a copy of the Spectrum ROM at address 0 but with the ability to poke, and alter, any ROM addresses. I, therefore, tried this out and found that indeed it did work.

However, in the process I discovered that data corruption occured in the character set and also in locations 0 to 4, and this warranted investigation.

The offending bits of code reside at locations 3372 and 13308/9.

The solution was quite simple.

Firstly, load a copy of the Spectrum's ROM into the SAM at 65536.

Then 'POKE 68908,23', DPOKE 78844,19

Next enter the following code in line 9999:-

```text
POKE 50000,1250,35,237,65,1,252,
4,237,65,199: CALL 50000
```

In a few moments your SAM becomes a Spectrum and you can alter ROM addresses to your heart's content.

One small restriction: don't try putting anything into locations 19 to 23 inclusive as these will be altered as the Spectrum runs.

Apart from this you can now POKE to ROM addresses to see what results.

NOW HERE'S A ROUTINE FOR THE SPECTRUM WHICH MAY BE OF INTEREST...

On the SAM there is a command 'INPUT #2;"name";a$', which results in the prompt appearing on the upper screen. Well, now we can have something comparable for the Spectrum. I've done it all in BASIC so that more users can see what's happening...

10 LET a=PEEK 23631+256*peek 23632.

20 POKE a+7,168: POKE a+8,16

30 INPUT#2;"name ";#0;a$: PRINT a$

40 INPUT#2;"age ";#0;b$:PRINT b$

50 INPUT#2;"sex ";#0;c$:PRINT c$ and so on.

As you will see, if you run this, the prompt will appear on the upper screen. Your response will be entered on the lower screen and will then be printed in the upper screen adjacent to the prompt.

An excellent way of entering multiple inputs.

You could try omitting the #0 in these lines but the results get very messy and need lots of '''' to tidy it up. you also get lots of cursors printed !!.

Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

The reason why I think nobody(?) has been aware of this is that it is possible on the SAM to "WRITE PROTECT" the RAM in the first page so that even machine code cannot write to it. This is done by setting bit 7 of the low memory page register (port 250).

Dark TO light is never right, Dark ON light is better.

I.e., print white, then yellow, then cyan, then magenta and lastly black. This way the lighter inks don't pick up the darker ones. It's easy when you think about it.

I got the idea watching a four- colour lithographic system in use. It also applies to some silk screen printing proccesses!

Dear Brian, I have a few programming hints and tips which might interest other readers, so thought I'd write in to share them. To begin with, I'd like to pass on two very useful pieces of inform- ation I received from a fellow OUTLET reader,Karl-Heinz Meander from Germany, who suggested I could forward them to you.

The first of these consists of two POKEs for 'Wordmaster' which will delete all files at once, saving having to do each one individually:

POKE 65532,158: POKE 65533,96.

These can be included permanent- ly as a final line in the 'Word- master' BASIC for convenience.

Secondly, Karl-Heinz has discovered two undocumented system variables in RAM page 7 of the 128K Spectrum which hold the colours used for the 128K Editor and Opening Menu. These can be altered from BASIC by a routine such as he suggests:-

10 CLEAR 49151 (or less) 20 POKE 23388,23 (page in Ram 7) 30 POKE 60431,main menu attribute byte 40 POKE 60433,editor attribute byte 50 POKE 23388,16 (page in Ram 0) 60 CLEAR 65367 (or whatever...)

Alternatively, I thought it might be an idea to set up these variables from machine-code, as this would get round the need to CLEAR 49151 first - not always convenient if included in a long program.

I have, therefore, written a short routine to demonstrate this [in ADD-ENDERS]then instead of having to work out the value of the attribute byte yourself, it is taken directly from ATTRP (23693).

All you need do, then, is set up the PAPER and INK commands as normal, then GOSUB 9910 (the line no. can be changed) which will make the colours in the 128K Editor & Menu the same.

(Please note, however, that even though this method makes it unnecessary to alter RAMTOP, the code in line 9910 still has to be below 49152 when called, to avoid paging itself out.)

Incidentally, the purpose of the variables temp1 and temp2 is for 48K compatibility, so that these locations will not be corrupted if paging does not take place.

What I cannot be certain of is whether these RAM 7 POKEs will work on +2A/+3 Spectrums, since Karl-Heinz, like myself, has the older type of 128K machine. (Perhaps you could let me know if it works on your own +3? I'd be interested to know.)

The other matter I wanted to mention concerns a peculiar hardware bug which affects certain Amstrad-made Spectrums (the grey +2s in particular) with certain programs, since it affected '$KIPPER' in the last issue. I have added a bit on to $KIPPER to overcome this problem on such machines.[In ADD-ENDERS]

Some people with grey +2s may have noticed that in 48 mode certain keys sometimes fail to respond as they should, namely the right and up arrow keys, caps shift/m, caps shift/n and symbol shift/a. Certain interfaces, particularly the Kempston Mouse, exacerbate the problem.

An intriguing fact, however, is that the symptoms are worst when the machine is first switched on, and gradually diminish as it warms up! I cannot shed much light on the actual cause of this, except to say that I once read somewhere that it was due to a bug in the ULA chip.

I discovered,through experiment, that the 'I' register plays an important role in these phenomena (though why this should be, I have no idea). When 'I' holds zero, the symptoms disappear completely. If 'I' holds 63, the arrow keys are not affected (at least on my machine), though the other keys I mentioned are.

If 'I' holds other values, the trouble is worst - hence the problem with $KIPPER on these machines (in 48 mode) - it uses interrupts and inhibits proper operation of these vital keys! My solution was to 'patch' a piece of code into the routine, temporarily loading 'I' with zero before calling the ROM key- scan (RST 56),which has cured the problem, at least for me. I shall find $KIPPER very useful as I frequently use the 48K editor for embedded codes, tokens etc. I don't know if you've heard of these effects before, but I know of other programs where these problems have arisen, and other people who have experienced them - notably with 'Wordmaster'.

(Incidentally, I wrote a 'patch' for Wordmaster to deal with this - if anyone wants it, please write to me with SAE.) I suspect many people probably (wrongly, though understandably) assume these things to be program bugs, whereas in reality it's the machine itself which is to blame.

(I wonder, does this also affect the +3 and +2A, or is it just the grey +2 models?)

Anyway, hope you will find these things useful, and keep up the good work.

Regards,

Miles Kinloch

Дальнейшее изучение кода управления страницами памяти навело меня на мысль, что должна существовать возможность поместить копию ROM Спектрума по адресу 0, но с возможностью изменять ячейки памяти через POKE. Поэтому я опробовал это и обнаружил, что это действительно работает.

Однако в процессе я заметил, что происходит повреждение данных в наборе символов, а также в ячейках с 0 по 4, и это потребовало разбирательства.

Виновные участки кода находились по адресам 3372 и 13308/9.

Решение оказалось довольно простым.

Во-первых, загрузите копию ROM Спектрума в SAM по адресу 65536.

Затем сделайте `POKE 68908,23`, `DPOKE 78844,19`.

Затем введите следующий код в строку 9999:

```text
POKE 50000,1250,35,237,65,1,252,4,237,65,199: CALL 50000
```

Через несколько мгновений ваш SAM превратится в Spectrum, и вы сможете изменять адреса ROM сколько душе угодно.

Одно небольшое ограничение: не пытайтесь ничего записывать в ячейки с 19 по 23 включительно, так как они будут перезаписываться во время работы Спектрума.

В остальном теперь вы можете применять POKE к адресам ROM и смотреть на результаты.

А ТЕПЕРЬ ПРОЦЕДУРА ДЛЯ SPECTRUM, КОТОРАЯ МОЖЕТ ОКАЗАТЬСЯ ИНТЕРЕСНОЙ...

На SAM есть команда `INPUT #2;"name";a$`, в результате которой приглашение ко вводу появляется на верхнем экране. Что ж, теперь у нас есть нечто подобное и для Spectrum. Я написал все на BASIC, чтобы больше пользователей могло понять, что происходит...

```text
10 LET a=PEEK 23631+256*PEEK 23632

20 POKE a+7,168: POKE a+8,16

30 INPUT #2;"name ";#0;a$: PRINT a$

40 INPUT #2;"age ";#0;b$: PRINT b$

50 INPUT #2;"sex ";#0;c$: PRINT c$
```
...и так далее.

Как вы увидите при запуске, приглашение ко вводу появится на верхнем экране. Ваш ответ будет вводиться на нижнем экране, а затем распечатается на верхнем рядом с приглашением.

Отличный способ для организации множественного ввода данных.

Вы можете попробовать убрать `#0` в этих строках, но результат станет очень неаккуратным и потребует множества `''''` для наведения порядка. Кроме того, напечатается куча курсоров!!

Тёмным ПО светлому — это правильно,  
Светлым ПО тёмному — никуда не годится.

То есть сначала печатайте белым, затем жёлтым, затем голубым (cyan), потом пурпурным (magenta) и напоследок чёрным. В этом случае более светлые чернила не пачкаются тёмными. Всё просто, если подумать.


Для удобства их можно внести на постоянной основе в качестве последней строки в BASIC-код 'Wordmaster'.

Во-вторых, Karl-Heinz обнаружил две недокументированные системные переменные в 7-й странице ОЗУ Spectrum 128K, которые хранят цвета, используемые для редактора 128K и стартового меню. Их можно изменить из BASIC с помощью предложенной им подпрограммы:

```text
10 CLEAR 49151 (или меньше)
20 POKE 23388,23 (подключить страницу Ram 7)
30 POKE 60431,байт атрибутов главного меню
40 POKE 60433,байт атрибутов редактора
50 POKE 23388,16 (подключить страницу Ram 0)
60 CLEAR 65367 (или сколько угодно...)
```

В качестве альтернативы я подумал, что было бы неплохо настраивать эти переменные из машинного кода, так как это избавило бы от необходимости предварительно делать CLEAR 49151 — что не всегда удобно в длинной программе.

Поэтому я написал короткую подпрограмму для демонстрации этого [в разделе ADD-ENDERS]. В ней значение байта атрибута не нужно высчитывать вручную — оно берётся напрямую из ATTRP (23693).

Всё, что вам нужно сделать — это настроить команды PAPER и INK как обычно, а затем выполнить GOSUB 9910 (номер строки можно изменить), что сделает цвета в редакторе 128K и меню такими же.

Кстати, назначение переменных temp1 и temp2 — совместимость с 48K, чтобы эти ячейки не испортились, если переключение страниц не произойдёт.
